Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, the expressions (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) are always equal. In floating-point arithmetic, however, most real numbers cannot be represented exactly, so each addition usually produces an intermediate result that must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Changing the grouping changes which intermediate values are formed and therefore where rounding occurs. The final results can consequently differ.

For example, if a is a very large positive number, b is the corresponding large negative number, and c is comparatively small, then (a + b) + c may preserve c because a and b cancel first. In a + (b + c), adding c to b may round away c before the cancellation occurs, producing a different answer. The precise outcome depends on the floating-point format, rounding mode, handling of subnormal values, and whether the processor uses operations such as fused multiply-add, which performs a multiplication and addition with only one final rounding.

Large matrix multiplications amplify the relevance of this behavior. Every output element is a dot product consisting of many products that must be summed. Although the mathematical sum is independent of order, the floating-point result is not. A sequential implementation might accumulate products from left to right, while a parallel implementation divides them among threads, computes partial sums, and combines those partial sums in a tree. GPUs, vectorized CPU kernels, and distributed systems may all use different partitions and reduction trees. Libraries may also select different algorithms according to matrix size, hardware, thread count, or workspace availability.

As a result, two executions of the same mathematical matrix multiplication can produce slightly different entries when they use different reduction orders. The differences are often only a few units in the last place, but they may become larger for long dot products or ill-conditioned data containing values with widely varying magnitudes or substantial cancellation. These small discrepancies can also propagate through later computations, especially iterative algorithms or decisions based on thresholds.

Reproducibility therefore requires more than using the same input data. It may require fixing the hardware, library version, thread count, kernel choice, and reduction order, while disabling nondeterministic algorithms. Stronger techniques include higher-precision accumulation, compensated or pairwise summation, and exact or reproducible accumulation schemes. These approaches improve consistency, but they can impose costs in speed, memory use, or implementation complexity.
